newsitem.title: AUSTRIA: Austria must opt for NATO after Paris pact-defmin.
newsitem.headline: Austria must opt for NATO after Paris pact-defmin.

text.p: Austria's Defence Minister Werner Fasslabend on Tuesday welcomed the NATO-Russia treaty as the beginning of a new era of cooperation in Europe and said neutral Austria could no longer remain on the sidelines.

Fasslabend, who belongs to the conservative People's Party in coalition with the Social Democrats, said the Founding Act signed in Paris formally ended an era of alliances forged after two world wars and heralded a future of integration.
"I believe this is the only way to secure a long-lasting, freely chosen peace," Fasslabend said in a statement.
"In this situation, we Austrians cannot and should not act as if it does not concern us, because today's event has decisive and fundamental consequences on our own security," he added.
"Austria can only have a negotiating role in the future if it is a member of NATO and the WEU (the Western European Union)," Fasslabend said.

Neutrality was enshrined in the constitution on the insistence of the Kremlin, which refused to pull its occupying troops out of Austria in 1955 unless the country rejected membership of military alliances. Austria was occupied by the World War Two victors after its defeat in 1945.
The People's Party, led by Foreign Minister Wolfgang Schuessel, has put pressure on the Social Democrats in the past few weeks to open a serious debate over whether to ditch neutrality and join NATO.

Conservatives, who back membership of the 16-nation alliance, have said a decision should be taken by the end of the year and at the latest before Austria assumes the European Union presidency in the second half of 1998.
Chancellor Viktor Klima's dominant Social Democrats want Austria to remain neutral and the NATO issue could seriously shake the already fractured coalition.
